title: How to give feedback that changes behaviour, not just feelings

audience.knows: Workplace conversations, with no prior feedback framework assumed
audience.cares_about: Addressing a colleague's behaviour without making the conversation only about personal reactions

outcome: Prepare feedback for a workplace situation, distinguish an actionable request from a personal judgment, and agree what to look for afterwards.
through_line: Make feedback a conversation about observable behaviour and a usable next step, rather than a verdict on the person.

arc_plan.what: Set up an explicitly imagined workplace feedback exchange in which the recipient cannot tell what to do differently; use this same situation throughout.
Establish the practical task: turn that unclear exchange into feedback the recipient can act on and the giver can follow up.
Rework the running exchange using the approved guidance on describing behaviour, inviting the recipient's perspective and agreeing a next step. Name each principle only after its use is visible.
arc_plan.needs: A reviewed knowledge sheet establishing an actionable feedback approach, its limitations and the criteria for an appropriate next step.

arc_plan.what: Ask the viewer to distinguish an actionable revision of the running exchange from a personal judgment, then explain the choice using the approved criteria.
arc_plan.needs: Reviewed criteria for judging feedback wording and a defensible explanation of the contrasting choices.

arc_plan.what: Have viewers prepare a feedback conversation of their own using the approved approach, including what change they would discuss and how they would revisit it.
arc_plan.needs: Reviewed application and follow-up guidance, including relevant limits on when ordinary colleague feedback is appropriate.

arc_plan.what: Return to the opening exchange with an actionable next step agreed; distinguish a clearer conversation from proof that behaviour has already changed.

must_cover.what: The distinction between feedback aimed at behaviour change and feedback focused only on personal reactions
An approved approach for describing workplace behaviour without substituting a judgment about the person
Guidance on inviting the recipient's perspective and agreeing an actionable next step
A meaningful check that asks viewers to judge feedback by its actionability, not recall terminology
Follow-up guidance and limits on what a feedback conversation can establish about subsequent behaviour change

must_avoid: Opening with terminology or an agenda
Guaranteeing that the right wording changes behaviour
Treating the recipient's feelings as irrelevant
Unrelated examples that replace the running situation
Presenting a proposed feedback framework as verified before knowledge review
example_posture: Use an explicitly imagined, ordinary colleague-to-colleague situation and return to it throughout. Keep the stakes proportionate and the recipient capable of responding; avoid caricatures, humiliation and invented success evidence. Any example dialogue is illustrative, not an authentic record of speech.
visual_direction: Use a cartoon workplace situation with a consistent pair of colleagues, a visible contrast between unclear and actionable feedback, and a simple view of the next step being agreed. Keep attention on the part of the exchange currently being discussed. Honour the requested story-cartoon direction while retaining a plain diagram-led alternative for later review.
voice_note: Sound like a warm mentor speaking to a capable colleague, not a teacher grading a learner. Keep the short lesson practical and conversational, allowing space for the viewer to make the check before the explanation.
open_questions: No factual feedback guidance or effectiveness claims have been verified. The proposed teaching approach, assessment criteria and follow-up guidance require an approved knowledge sheet before scripting.
The requester has not specified a feedback framework or exclusions. Should the lesson stay with routine peer feedback, or address manager feedback as well?
The story-cartoon request does not settle whether people should act out exchanges or appear as illustrated faces; retain both options for review.
